stem: A histogram is drawn for marks scored by 100 students. The class interval 0-20 has a frequency density of 3 per mark. The interval 20-30 has a frequency density of 2 per mark. The interval 30-40 has a frequency density of 1 per mark. The interval 40-50 has a frequency density of 1 per mark. How many students scored marks in the class 0-20?

per_option_rationale.rationale: The student multiplies frequency density 3 by width 10 instead of the correct width 20, giving 3 * 10 = 30.
The student uses the density of the adjacent class (2 per mark for 20-30) and multiplies by the correct width 20, giving 2 * 20 = 40.
The student divides frequency density by class width instead of multiplying: 3 / 20 = 0.15, then scales by 100, giving 15.
Frequency = frequency density * class width = 3 * 20 = 60 students.

explanation: In a histogram with unequal class widths, frequency = frequency density * class width. The class 0-20 has width 20 and density 3, so frequency = 3 * 20 = 60.

explanation_sections.punchline: Frequency = frequency density * class width. Width of 0-20 is 20, not 10. So frequency = 3 * 20 = 60.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: in a histogram with unequal class widths, bar height = frequency density = frequency / class width. To recover frequency, multiply density by width. Decisive move: read the class width directly from the boundaries (20 - 0 = 20), not by assuming all widths are equal. For class 0-20: frequency = 3 * 20 = 60. Verify by computing all classes: 3*20 + 2*10 + 1*10 + 1*10 = 60+20+10+10 = 100 total students confirmed.
explanation_sections.lesson: The most common trap is reading the class width as 10 (matching the other equal-width classes) instead of 20. Option 1 (30 = 3*10) captures exactly this error. When class widths differ, compute each width separately from its boundaries.
explanation_sections.timing: 75 seconds. Read class width 20-0=20 (5 seconds). Multiply 3*20=60 (5 seconds). Cross-check by summing all four class frequencies to confirm total = 100 (30 seconds).
